2) Concurrency & throughput: approximate concurrent user sessions and expected peak RPS during day peaks. You mentioned ~50-100 concurrent users and ~100 req/s peak — please confirm.

4) Typical payload sizes: average input tokens, average output tokens, and worst-case document sizes.
5) Benchmarks: please share a sample payload (anonymized) and a 48-hour traffic profile so we can run a representative bench.

Hi Marissa — thanks for the recap, that matches our discussion. Quick answers below, and a few clarifying Qs.

1) Latency: we are aiming for p95 <= 300ms and p50 <= 120ms for the interactive workflow. For background/batch jobs, higher latency is OK.
2) Concurrency/Throughput: estimate ~50-100 concurrent UI sessions, peak ~100 req/s across the org during market open.
3) Streaming: important for the UI chat flow (users should see partial tokens quickly). For document synthesis, streaming is nice-to-have but not required.
4) Payload sizes: average input ~600 tokens, average output ~200 tokens. We do have use cases where users upload long documents (10k+ tokens) and want a single synthesized answer — these are less frequent (~2% of requests) but important.

Clarifying Qs:
- Does Redwood support 32k context today for the recommended models, and what is the expected impact on p95 if we use 32k vs 16k?
- For streaming, what kind of startup latency (first token) should we expect vs overall completion time for long outputs?

Hi team — thanks for the details, Mike. A few technical notes and a proposed plan. I'll keep this high level and then we can run a targeted bench with your sample payload.

Redwood support & recommended profiles:
- Context windows: we support model variants with 8k, 16k, and 32k context. For production SLOs at the scale you described, we typically recommend testing the 16k profile first and running a small 32k pilot for long-doc use cases.

Latency guidance (typical observed p95 in our internal benches on GPU-optimized runtime; numbers are indicative and depend on exact model, tokenization, and batching):
- 8k context (average request 600+200 tokens): p95 ~ 150-200 ms (single-request path, minimal batching).
- 16k context: p95 ~ 200-260 ms.
- 32k context: p95 can increase to ~350-450 ms for single-request paths, primarily due to longer KV/cache management and memory pressure — this is the main cause of the step-up.

Notes on streaming vs blocking responses:
- Streaming (token-by-token) improves perceived latency: first token can often be returned in ~80-120 ms for small outputs on the 8k/16k profiles. For large outputs (1k+ tokens) streaming lets the UI show progress while generation continues; total completion time still reflects total tokens generated.
- For 32k contexts, first-token streaming may still appear in ~120-200 ms, but the backend CPU/GPU scheduling and larger attention windows increase variance, so p95 can be higher.

Throughput & concurrency tradeoffs:
- Batching increases throughput but can add queuing latency; we recommend adaptive batching with latency SLOs (max batch delay 10-20 ms) for your interactive endpoints.
- For ~100 req/s and 50-100 concurrent sessions: with a 16k profile and adaptive batching you should expect to meet the p95 <= 300ms target with conservative autoscaling knobs.

Suggested immediate plan:
1) Fill the attached SLO matrix (Marissa's file). We'll use it to configure bench targets.
2) Run a 2-hour bench: replicate your peak-rate traffic + a 30-minute long-doc stress (10k-32k inputs at low QPS) to capture worst-case tails.
3) Deliver a bench report: p50/p95/p99 latency, per-token cost estimate, memory/burst behavior, and recommended model/quantization profile.

Attached: redwood_latency_matrix_q1_2027.pdf (sample bench report & latency curves).

Would be great to get the sample payload and a 48-hour traffic profile so we can schedule the bench for early next week. I can run the bench and share a recording of the run.

Cheers,
